analysis.one_liner: Replaces the free-claim hardrock mining system with leases, royalties, and cleanup funding on federal land.
analysis.headline: A House committee approved the mining overhaul 21-13 and reported it to the full House in August 2020, but the House never voted on it before the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would end the 1872-era system that lets companies stake hardrock mining claims on federal land without paying royalties, and would eventually bar them from converting those claims into private ownership of the land. Instead, miners would get leases and pay a 12.5% royalty on new operations and at least 8% on existing ones, with an exemption for small miners. It would bar mining in sacred sites, wilderness study areas, critical habitat, and other protected places, require consultation with Indian tribes before mining that could affect tribal lands, require cleanup bonds from operators, and channel mining revenue into a fund to clean up abandoned mines.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who use public lands and waters in mining states, Indian tribes whose lands and sacred sites sit near mining activity, and taxpayers. A quarter of the mining revenue would go to state governments, and the rest would fund reclamation of abandoned mines whose cleanup costs now fall on the public.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Public lands users, tribes, and taxpayers

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a first-ever 12.5% royalty on new hardrock mining operations and at least an 8% royalty on existing ones, ending the practice of mining gold, silver, and copper on federal land without paying the government, with an exemption for small miners.
Prohibits issuing new patents for mining and millsite claims, ending the ability of companies to turn federal mining claims into outright private ownership of the land.

Bars hardrock mining in sacred sites, wilderness study areas, critical habitat, roadless areas, and other protected places, and requires a suitability finding before mining near aquifers, historic places, and conservation areas.

Requires agencies to consult Indian tribes before any mineral activity that could substantially affect tribal lands or interests, and protects sensitive tribal information such as sacred site locations from public disclosure.
Creates a Hardrock Minerals Reclamation Fund to clean up and restore land and water damaged by past hardrock mining, and requires operators to post financial assurance for cleanup before operating.
Sends 25% of mining revenues, fees, and penalties to the states where the mining occurs, with the remainder deposited into the reclamation fund.

analysis.who_pays: Hardrock mining companies operating on federal land, which would pay royalties for the first time, obtain leases and permits instead of self-initiated claims, cap their holdings at 20,480 acres per state, post cleanup bonds, and lose the ability to patent claims into private land.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hardrock mining companies on federal land

drawbacks.text: New royalties, lease rentals, permitting requirements, and acreage caps would raise the cost of mining on federal land; defenders of the current system argue this could reduce domestic production of metals like copper and gold and cost mining jobs in western states.

Existing mining operations with approved plans are effectively grandfathered for up to 10 years, and nonproducing claims likewise get up to a decade to convert to leases, so the biggest environmental and revenue changes would phase in slowly.

The bill lets the Secretary reduce the royalty floor to 6.25% for operations that claim they cannot produce without a reduction, or to encourage strategic and critical minerals, creating room for the same negotiating pressure the bill is meant to end.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs fall almost entirely on mining companies that today extract billions of dollars in minerals from public land without paying royalties, while the benefits — cleanup of abandoned mines, protection of water and sacred sites, and revenue to states and the Treasury — accrue to the public. The tradeoff for consumers is modest and indirect: mineral prices could rise slightly if royalties are passed through. The bill's main design weakness is its long phase-in for existing claims and operations, which delays the largest gains.

outcome.mechanism: The House Natural Resources Committee approved and reported the bill and placed it on the House calendar, but House leaders never brought it to the floor for a vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 8, 2019 by Rep. Raúl Grijalva with 15 original cosponsors and referred to the House Natural Resources Committee.
On October 23, 2019, the committee ordered the bill reported in amended form by a vote of 21-13 after a markup session, discharging the Energy and Mineral Resources subcommittee.
The committee reported the bill on August 4, 2020 with an amendment, House Report 116-467, and it was placed on the Union Calendar as Calendar No. 374.

By the time sponsor additions were recorded on August 4, 2020, the bill had 27 Democratic cosponsors beyond its sponsor; no further House action was taken, and the Congress ended January 3, 2021 without a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hardrock mining companies came out ahead: they continue to mine gold, copper, and other metals on federal land under the 1872 law without paying royalties, can still patent claims into private ownership where pending, and face no new cleanup-bond or leasing requirements. Taxpayers continue to carry the cost of cleaning up abandoned hardrock mines, and the reclamation fund the bill would have created was never funded.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hardrock mining companies still mining royalty-free

for.name: Raúl Grijalva
for.role: Chair, House Natural Resources Committee; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, chaired the committee that marked it up and reported it to the House.

for.name: 27 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, adding 12 more names when it was reported in August 2020.

for.name: House Natural Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Held a subcommittee hearing, discharged the subcommittee, approved the bill in a 21-13 markup vote, and reported it amended.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a vote on the House floor after it was reported and placed on the calendar; it died there when the Congress ended.

against.name: Hardrock mining industry
against.role: Gold, copper, and other metal producers on federal land
against.what_they_did: Opposed hardrock mining royalty and leasing legislation in Congress, an industry-wide position that has kept similar reforms from reaching floor votes for decades.

sides.party_line_note: Every House sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat, and the committee's 21-13 vote to report the bill split closely along party lines, with the 13 no votes coming from the committee's Republican minority.

industries.industry: Hardrock mining companies (gold, copper, silver, and other metal producers on federal land)
industries.note: The bill would end royalty-free extraction of public minerals, require leases and cleanup bonds, cap holdings, and block patenting of claims into private land — costs the industry has avoided under the 1872 Mining Law. Its gain in keeping the status quo is the public's loss in unpaid royalties and unfunded mine cleanup.

industries.industry: State governments in western mining states
industries.note: Would receive 25% of royalties, fees, and penalties from mining on federal land within their borders, revenue they currently do not collect.
A dedicated reclamation fund would finance cleanup of abandoned hardrock mines, creating sustained public work restoring land and water.
